set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, or with different music. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.
set.magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613.
set.exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions (one standard playlist, with one exception), as patients described it a week later; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
set.comparator: None for music itself: every patient heard music; patients who described it less favourably, and panel respondents who did not name the music
set.outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire); thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: 19 patients; the interval for the main correlation runs from 0.20 to 0.83; the panel's harm estimate for music rests on 30 people (interval 0.87 to 8.21).
set.grade.reasoning: Correlational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). Status single study: the music-outcome association rests on one small trial; the panel survey adds only null associations, one of them very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card in this round. A randomized comparison of musical genres in psilocybin sessions (Strickland et al., 2021) is on the project's list and has not yet been read; by its title it compares genres, not music with silence.

evidence_set: Methods › Participants; Experiment overview and procedures, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; The semi-structured interview, 1st paragraph

Percentage fall in QIDS at one week correlated with interview-rated music liking r = 0.60, resonance r = 0.59 and openness r = 0.57, but not with self-rated drug intensity (r = 0.004); n = 19. Editors' 95% intervals (Fisher z): 0.20 to 0.83, 0.19 to 0.82, 0.16 to 0.81 and −0.45 to 0.46. The music ratings come from interviews at the same time point as the QIDS outcome, one week after the second session (the paper does not say it was the same visit).

Agreement between the four raters averaged r = 0.6 (± 0.1, not stated to be an SD), which the authors call good; the three music ratings correlated r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91 with each other, and the authors note they probably represent one construct.

evidence_add.extracted: A standardized playlist was intended for all patients; one patient (#6), who strongly disliked the music in the first session, heard a playlist used at Johns Hopkins University in the second session.

set.statement: As described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session goes. The review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn; a randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression published after that search (Greenway et al., 2024) has not yet been read for this answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: A review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all with patients. Most gave ketamine together with other medicines, usually during surgery or tests; in most of these, music went with less worry or pain. Only one study of ketamine alone compared listening with silence: children who heard their mother's voice were less anxious. The review, searched to the end of 2023, found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression, so it is not known whether music helps; a trial published in 2024 has not been read here yet.
set.magnitude: No pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.
set.comparator: No music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies
set.grade.reasoning: For the question asked (music in ketamine sessions), the primary evidence the review describes is small trials of unstated design, case reports and interview studies, so it starts low; down one for risk of bias (not appraisable) and one for indirectness (second-hand, procedural, with other drugs), giving very low. Status single study: for ketamine or esketamine alone the review found one comparison of listening with no listening (46 children under anaesthesia, hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review; the procedural trials gave ketamine with other drugs. The claim rests only on a scoping review, recorded as a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). A randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression (Greenway et al., 2024, on the project's list) appeared after the review's search; it has no card in this round, and this answer should be revisited when it has been read.

evidence_set: Only ketamine-alone study that compared a listening group with a group that heard nothing: 46 children having cardiac catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia; 23 heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12, non-musical in 8, mixed in 3) and had lower preoperative anxiety and fewer emergence reactions and less agitation than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The others: a single-case report, a two-patient case report and two qualitative studies (17 and 12 people); for the 17-person study Table 1 records a control group without saying how many listened to music, and no music comparison is reported.

Qualitative: in 17 people with treatment-resistant depression on oral esketamine, music was described as blocking distractions and deepening internal exploration, while some felt it kept them tethered to the outside world (3.2.1) and one participant stopped using it for that reason (Table 1); in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, all who listened had auditory distortions (shifts in speed and pitch), felt as positive or negative depending on their state.

Combination studies (ketamine with other sedatives or analgesics, in procedures or, in one study, air medical transport): music went with less intraoperative sedation, lower anxiety, pain or fear, and lower drug use in most; one trial found no effect on emergence reactions; another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music but no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams.

set.statement: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who took MDMA by mouth lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; a single dose in each analysed session, 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; 112 of them also took MDMA in another session after a medicine given first, which was not analysed; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, among them any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, feeling stimulated and liking, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism (rated at screening) and trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the dose with more anxiety (0.25 and 0.23); oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, impaired control and anxiety were rated on a questionnaire at the end of the session, looking back over it. Each of these associations survived correction for multiple testing and was modest, explaining 5 to 12% of the variation (semi-partial R2). For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest in the penalized models, but the association with age did not survive correction for multiple testing in the main models. Women and men did not differ significantly once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, so sex and dose per kilogram went together and cannot be cleanly separated in these data (dose per kilogram varied from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg across the volunteers). The authors note that this does not confirm earlier studies that found differences between women and men even after adjusting for body weight, and they cite others, among them an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), suggesting that women may be more prone to unpleasant effects, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people detected no differences between women and men. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times before the study. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, highly standardized, could not be studied. So differences between bodies went with feeling more or less from the same amount: at a fixed amount a lighter body meant more per kilogram, which went with stronger effects, and genetically lower enzyme activity went with a higher blood level; each analysed session had one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In laboratory studies of healthy young adults, how much MDMA they got for their body weight, and how much reached the blood, went most with how strongly they felt it. People with more anxious personalities, or who felt anxious and low just before, said at the end of the session that they had felt more anxious, and more open people felt closer to others; these links were modest. Women and men did not clearly differ once body weight was allowed for, although an earlier report from the same laboratory suggested women may feel more unpleasant effects. Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
set.magnitude: Unadjusted: blood level and any drug effect beta 0.48. Penalized models: dose per kilogram selected for 21 of 25 responses, first for 12. Adjusted for dose per kilogram and corrected for multiple testing: CYP2D6 genetic activity score and blood level −0.19 (R2 0.10); age and heart-rate rise −0.27 (R2 0.07); openness and closeness 0.28 (R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (R2 0.06); neuroticism and trait anxiety and dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (R2 0.12 and 0.11), impaired control 0.26 each; anxious-depressed and introverted mood before the dose and 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (R2 0.06 and 0.05). Age and bad drug effect: first in the penalized model, not significant after correction. Sex and previous MDMA use (at most five times): no significant association after adjustment.
set.exposure: Dose per kilogram and, without adjustment, blood level; characteristics measured before dosing: sex, age, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, previous MDMA use, personality at screening, trait anxiety (timing not stated) and mood just before the dose
set.outcome: Self-rated and physical effects of MDMA (visual analogue scales over the session; 5D-ASC rated at the end of the session, looking back; Adjective Mood Rating Scale; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood level)
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns (card sc_studerus_2021): each predictor adjusted only for dose per kilogram, correlated predictors not adjusted for one another, blinding probably did not hold at 125 mg, the text does not say whether ratings were placebo-corrected, so rating style could add to trait-rating associations, and the 5D-ASC ratings were made at the end of the session, looking back.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: One pooled analysis. On sex, the authors cite an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017) among studies suggesting women may be more prone to unpleasant effects; the two analyses share most of their data and are not independent, so this is stated in the claim rather than rated as inconsistency.
set.grade.reasoning: The MDMA-placebo contrast was randomized in each source study, but which person's characteristics predict the response is a between-person, observational question, so it starts low; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: one pooled analysis from one laboratory; other Basel pooled analyses share these source studies and its LSD counterpart shares one study and several authors, so they are not independent confirmation. On sex, the answer on what MDMA feels like reports the earlier analysis (higher bad-effect ratings in women after allowing for dose per kilogram); in the editors' reading the difference may come from the outcome measure (area under the effect curve here, peak ratings there) and from the correction for multiple testing applied here, and it is listed for the senior author.

evidence_set: Mood immediately before intake: more anxiety-depressiveness and more introversion predicted higher 5D-ASC anxiety scores (beta 0.25 and 0.23; R2 0.06 and 0.05); the 5D-ASC was completed 6 h after dosing, rating the session retrospectively.
Results, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Predictor variables, 5th paragraph; Methods › Response variables, 4th paragraph

Sex was not significantly associated with any response after adjustment for dose per body weight; the authors attribute women's stronger unadjusted response to their higher dose per kilogram (fixed doses, lower body weight).

evidence_add.extracted: Older age went with a smaller rise in body temperature, less liking and good drug effect, a smaller decrease in general inactivation and more bad drug effect, but these associations did not withstand correction for multiple testing; the age range was limited (people over 45 excluded).

set.statement: In 213 healthy volunteers aged 25 to 64 (108 women) who took LSD mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present (some sessions included an MRI scan), and placebo on another day in eight of the nine studies (nine double-blind crossover studies pooled by the Basel laboratory that ran them, 297 LSD sessions; one dose by mouth per session, 25 to 200 micrograms, as study conditions; Vizeli et al., 2024), the dose given was the strongest predictor of almost every effect compared with placebo, and characteristics measured before the dose were also associated with the response at a given dose: higher well-being rated just before, with stronger subjective effects in general, by the Discussion's summary (it was significantly associated with every self-rated scale, the anxiety-type scales included, except a bad drug effect and two others; the direction scale by scale is shown only in a figure not read); anxiety rated just before, with more anxiety during the session; openness, with more mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion, with more visual and auditory changes; more previous hallucinogen experience, with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; and genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with higher blood levels of LSD and more anxious ego dissolution. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any effect. Older age went with more, and higher body weight with less, bad drug effect, and women had smaller increases than men in four positive ratings and in body temperature; women's slightly less positive ratings were not significant when one dose per study was analysed (the text does not say whether the temperature difference held), and the abstract's statement that sex and body weight had no significant influence does not match the main results. The text gives the direction and significance of each association after correction for 551 tests but no sizes, which are only in a figure and a supplement not read here, so how much any characteristic other than dose matters cannot be said; bad drug effects were generally small. Expectations were not among the 19 predictors, and the setting barely varied. Genes for the CYP2D6 enzyme and earlier hallucinogen use went with feeling more or less from the same amount; earlier use was compared between people, so it cannot show that use itself changed the response. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In laboratory studies of healthy adults, the LSD dose was linked most closely to how strong the effects were. People who felt well just before had stronger effects, people who felt anxious had more anxiety, open personalities had more mystical feelings, and people who had used hallucinogens more often had a smaller overall effect. The paper gives the direction of each link but not its size. Everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
set.magnitude: Directions and corrected significance only; no sizes in the text. Dose strongest for every effect except body temperature (selected by LASSO for all 29 responses, largest for 21). Pre-drug well-being: significant for all subjective scales except bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, with effects more pronounced at higher well-being by the Discussion's summary; pre-drug anxiety: more 5D-ASC anxiety; openness: mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion: visual and auditory changes; previous hallucinogen experience: smaller 5D-ASC total, less anxious ego dissolution; lower CYP2D6 genetic activity score: higher plasma LSD and more anxious ego dissolution; age more and body weight less bad drug effect; women smaller increases in four positive ratings (not significant in the one-dose sensitivity analysis) and in temperature (not reported there).
set.exposure: Characteristics measured before dosing: dose, mood just before the dose, personality, previous hallucinogen experience, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, age, sex and body weight; whether the session included an MRI scan

evidence_add.extracted: The authors summarize that the subjective effects were more pronounced in people with higher ratings of well-being, extraversion, emotional excitability, activity or anxiety before drug intake, and that women reported a slightly less positive experience, a difference not statistically significant in the one-dose-per-study sensitivity analysis.
